title: Nanoscale Properties of Cortical Bone Tissue within Peri-lacunar Regions
content: This study describes nanoIR and nanoindentation techniques to map the compositional and material strength properties of bone biopsy tissue at the osteocyte peri-lacunar regions. Osteocytes play a vital role in bone remodeling, sensing mechanical strain, and regulating matrix production, mineralization, and resorption. This study explores their contribution to bone fragility in postmenopausal women with long-term Type-1 diabetes (T1D), hypothesizing that altered mineral/matrix composition within peri-lacunar regions contributes to fragility [1-2]. nanoIR was used to overcome the limitations of traditional methods (e.g., FTIR, AFM, SEM, TEM) by enabling nanoscale compositional mapping [3-4]. Bone biopsies from the iliac crest of T1D patients and controls were analyzed, with spectra collected over 1900–922 cm−¹, normalized for peak amplitude, and averaged for noise reduction. Two approaches were employed: (1) IR mapping of phosphate I (1030 cm−¹), phosphate II (1110 cm−¹), and amide I (1644 cm−¹), and (2) a 7×7 localized IR array spanning 70×70 μm around lacunae, with 10 μm spacing. Spectral data up to ∼85 μm from lacunae were processed using MATLAB for trapezoidal integration. Mineral-to-matrix (MM) ratios were calculated by dividing phosphate (1140–950 cm−¹) by amide I (1720–1600 cm−¹) areas, while matrix maturity crystallinity (mmc) ratios were determined by dividing apatitic phosphate (1030 cm−¹) by non-apatitic phosphate (1110 cm−¹) peak areas. This approach provides insights into bone fragility mechanisms linked to osteocyte function and peri-lacunar composition. Figure 1a shows an AFM height image with a lacuna in the lower-left corner and a 7×7 array of nanoIR spectral positions. Figure 1b displays 49 localized nanoIR spectra from the array, revealing compositional variation. Figure 1c illustrates the apatitic phosphate I intensity map, representing the primary inorganic phase of the mineralized bone, with higher values indicating regions of greater mineral density. Figure 1d shows the non-apatitic phosphate II intensity map, reflecting less-ordered mineral phases that complement the apatitic phosphate and provide insight into mineral heterogeneity. Figure 1e is the map of the amide I intensity, which corresponds to the organic matrix, primarily collagen, highlighting the spatial distribution of protein content. Figure 1f displays the MM ratio map, a mineral content metric that uniquely takes into account the amount of matrix present in the volume analyzed. Figure 1g presents the MMC ratio map, highlighting the degree of crystallographic order in the mineral phase, where higher values indicate more mature and crystalline structures. The mapping reveals lower MMC values near lacunae and higher values further away. Together, these mappings provide a comprehensive view of the spatial variation in mineral and organic composition, as well as the mineral quality, in the bone matrix surrounding the lacuna.
